papers.title: A live online exercise program for older adults improves depression and life-space mobility: A mixed-methods pilot randomized controlled trial
papers.quartile: Q1 (SJR 2024, Multidisciplinary; not in Psychiatry and Mental Health)
papers.introduction: The primary aim was to test the preliminary effectiveness of a live online exercise program led by qualified instructors on older adults’ physical activity levels, compared with a waitlist control group.
papers.methodology: Pilot convergent parallel mixed-methods RCT. Community-dwelling women and men aged 65 to 80 were randomized to an 8-week live online exercise program delivered on Zoom (ACTIVE) or a waitlist control (CON). Data came from an accelerometer, questionnaires and interviews. Pre-to-post changes were analyzed with a two-way repeated measures ANOVA; interviews were thematically analyzed in Dedoose.
papers.theory: Guided by the CONSORT 2010 statement: extension for pilot and feasibility trials. No theory is named.
papers.results: In the ACTIVE group, depressive symptoms decreased pre to post intervention (interaction p = 0.012) and life-space mobility increased (interaction p = 0.014). There were no significant between- or within-group differences for anxiety or loneliness, and no between-group differences in daily steps or nutrition risk. Attendance was 97% in the ACTIVE group.
papers.discussion: The authors report that the program did not affect habitual physical activity but reduced depressive symptoms and improved life-space mobility, with excellent adherence and acceptability. They describe online exercise programs as viable service-delivery options, particularly when in-person programming is unavailable.
papers.limitations: The authors acknowledge a small sample, which left the pilot underpowered for its primary outcome, and a lack of blinding of assessors and participants. They note the sample included only English-speaking people with home internet access. They suggest future studies include marginalized populations and different language options, including subtitles.

papers.title: Effectiveness of exercise-based rehabilitation for depressive symptoms, anxiety, and health-related quality of life in adults with rheumatoid arthritis: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
papers.quartile: Q1 (SJR 2025, Multidisciplinary; not in Psychiatry and Mental Health)
papers.introduction: The review aimed to evaluate the effects of structured exercise on depressive symptoms, anxiety and health-related quality of life in adults with rheumatoid arthritis. Where sufficient data were available, it also examined whether effects differed between conventional and mind-body exercise.
papers.methodology: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials of adults with rheumatoid arthritis, conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020. Two reviewers independently screened studies and extracted data. Searches ran to 26 November 2025, and only English-language articles were eligible. Random-effects meta-analyses used Hedges’ g in RevMan 5.4; risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2 and certainty of evidence with GRADE.
papers.results: Fifteen trials with 1652 participants were included. Structured exercise was associated with lower depressive symptom scores (SMD = −0.49; P < 0.001), lower anxiety scores (SMD = −0.45; P < 0.001) and better QoL/HRQoL (SMD = 0.45; P = 0.001). Certainty was rated moderate for depressive symptoms and low for anxiety and HRQoL. Conventional and mind-body exercise did not differ significantly.
papers.discussion: The authors conclude that structured exercise is a reasonable adjunct to comprehensive RA care for depressive symptoms, anxiety and perceived health status. They state that it should not replace pharmacologic disease control or formal mental-health care when these are indicated, and that the evidence is promising but not definitive.
papers.limitations: The authors note that the trials were generally small and varied in intervention, comparator and outcome instruments, and that most outcomes were self-reported with blinding usually infeasible. Few studies per outcome limited subgroup precision and publication-bias assessment. Most analyses used immediate post-intervention outcomes, so durability is uncertain. Only English-language articles were included, which may have introduced language bias.

introduction.q: Accordingly, this systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the effects of structured exercise interventions on depressive symptoms, anxiety, and HRQoL in adults with RA.

papers.title: Physical activity and depressive symptoms among college students: positive mental health as a mediator
papers.quartile: Q1 (SJR 2025, Psychology (miscellaneous); not in Psychiatry and Mental Health)
papers.introduction: The study tests whether positive mental health mediates the link between physical activity and depressive symptoms among college students. Depressive symptoms are described as a pressing global public health challenge and the most prevalent mental health disorder among college students.
papers.methodology: Cross-sectional online survey of 3,140 Chinese college students, recruited by convenience sampling between May and June 2025 and aged 18–27. Measures were the PARS-3 (α = 0.634), the Positive Mental Health Scale (α = 0.95) and the PHQ-9 (α = 0.935). Analysis used Spearman correlations and PROCESS Model 4 with 5,000 bootstrap resamples, controlling for age, gender, grade and educational level.
papers.theory: The study is anchored in Self-Determination Theory, which names autonomy, competence and relatedness as three innate psychological needs critical to high-quality motivation and psychological well-being.
papers.results: Physical activity was significantly associated with depressive symptoms in total (c = −0.015, p < 0.01). The indirect effect through positive mental health was significant (ab = −0.007, 95% CI [−0.010, −0.004]), while the direct effect was not significant (c' = −0.008, p = 0.080). Positive mental health was negatively associated with depressive symptoms (b = −0.250, p < 0.001).
papers.discussion: The authors read the results as a small indirect association consistent with a mediation pattern, with positive mental health as a possible mediator. They propose positive mental health as a useful conceptual focus for future research and a multi-tiered strategy for colleges to integrate physical activity into mental health promotion.
papers.limitations: The authors note that the cross-sectional design prevents confirmation of causal sequences, that self-reported positive mental health may not capture culturally distinct well-being, that PARS-3 reliability was modest (α = 0.634), that convenience sampling limits generalizability, and that the variance explained was low (R2 = 0.014). Suggested directions include longitudinal experience-sampling studies, mixed-methods work, PARS-3 validation, replication in probabilistic samples and cross-cultural validation.

papers.quartile: Q1 (SJR 2023, Medicine (miscellaneous); not in Psychiatry and Mental Health)
papers.introduction: The study aimed to make a preliminary assessment of depression rates, physical activity levels and the link between them among students in Poland and Portugal in the further year of the COVID-19 pandemic. It notes that restrictions during the pandemic have largely led to a decline in daily physical activity.
papers.methodology: Online cross-sectional survey in October 2022 of 398 students (229 from Poland, 169 from Portugal) aged 17 to 26, distributed through a Google form link on e-learning platforms and Facebook groups. Depression was measured with the Beck Depression Inventory and physical activity with an abbreviated IPAQ, each in Polish and Portuguese. papers.results: Moderate depression affected 20–35% of respondents, and depression classification did not differ between countries. papers.discussion: The authors report a tendency for depression severity to fall as physical activity rises, with a stronger effect in men. They state that there are not many statistically significant differences in depression and physical activity between Polish and Portuguese students, and call for further research on the optimal activity level.
papers.limitations: The authors note that the cross-sectional design does not give robust causal evidence, that the sample was small and the findings preliminary, that the online format means respondents' identity is unknown, that social media may attract stressed individuals and affect representativeness, and that self-report may bias responses. papers.title: Experiences of exercise and mental well-being among psychiatric inpatients: a qualitative study
papers.introduction: The study explores how psychiatric inpatients experience exercise and its perceived impact on mental well-being during hospitalization. Research on exercise specifically among psychiatric inpatients is described as limited, and less is known about how these patients experience it.
papers.methodology: Qualitative study of eight inpatients (five male, three female; mean age 53.9, range 31 to 84) at the University Hospital of North Norway, recruited by purposive sampling after completing at least two supported exercise sessions. Each took part in a semi-structured telephone interview of about 30 minutes, audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim. Transcripts were analysed with reflexive thematic analysis using a six-step approach.
papers.theory: The analysis took a contextualist perspective. Behavioral activation is offered as one possible interpretation of the findings.
papers.results: Four themes were identified: follow-up support, symptom reduction, sense of mastery and activation during hospitalization. Participants described improvements in mood after exercise and said the exercise physiologist was a crucial source of support. The perceived effects were not uniformly strong, and some participants were uncertain about effects on sleep or energy.
papers.discussion: The authors describe exercise as having a positive role in participants' perceived mental state, while stating that the findings reflect subjective experiences and are not evidence of treatment efficacy or causal effects. They suggest that structured exercise with professional support may be valuable, and that more inpatients may need the opportunity to exercise regularly.
papers.limitations: The authors note the small sample of eight, the difficulty of recruiting a diverse sample, a possible selection and social desirability bias because an exercise physiologist recruited participants, the lack of a comparator that would separate exercise from other treatment, the heterogeneity of diagnoses, telephone interviews that limit non-verbal cues, and a single Norwegian centre. Future research is to examine efficacy, identify active components and use broader, more diverse samples.

papers.title: Improvements in physical activity and depression symptoms: an observational study of users of a multi-modal digital mental health platform
papers.quartile: Q1 (SJR 2025, Biomedical Engineering; 3 other categories also Q1; not in Psychiatry and Mental Health)
papers.introduction: The study examined depression and physical activity among employees using an employer-sponsored digital mental health platform. Its three aims were baseline prevalence, baseline links between the two, and change over time.
papers.methodology: Prospective observational study of individuals who recently sought services through an employer-sponsored digital mental health platform, conducted September 2021 to May 2022. Adults aged 18 or older living in the United States; 755 at baseline and 480 in longitudinal analyses. Physical activity was measured with the IPAQ-Short Form, depression with the PHQ-9, and perceived mental health impact with one self-report item. Analyses used R and paired t-tests.
papers.results: 47.3% of the 755 baseline adults were underactive. Men reported more physical activity than women. Women and non-binary adults reported higher PHQ-9 scores than men, a difference the authors call statistically but not clinically significant. Physical activity was negatively correlated with PHQ-9 scores. Among underactive participants, MVPA rose by an average of 60 min per week and PHQ-9 fell by 2.8 points.
papers.discussion: The authors report that participants with elevated depression improved significantly, while nearly all with low baseline symptoms stayed asymptomatic. They suggest digital mental health platforms can support both symptom improvement and maintenance, and that multi-modal support may have reinforced physical activity.
papers.limitations: The authors note the observational design could not determine the temporal sequence of changes or causality, and call for an experimental design. They also flag an unvalidated single-item measure, the PHQ-9 cut-off, unexamined industry differences, missing implementation factors, and limited generalizability. They suggest follow-up of perhaps 6 or 12 months.

papers.introduction: The proposed review aims to investigate the effects of chronic exercise on overall depression severity and on different depressive symptoms in older adults with a mean age of at least 60, in randomized controlled trials. It will also consider how intervention and individual characteristics moderate these effects.
papers.methodology: Protocol for a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials, following PRISMA-P. Several electronic databases will be searched from inception. Pairs of reviewers will select studies, extract data and assess quality. A random-effects model will be used, with Hedges’ g as the summary effect.

papers.limitations: The authors plan to exclude RCTs testing pharmacological treatment and/or psychotherapy, so no conclusions can be drawn for add-on treatment; they acknowledge possibly missing relevant insights. They anticipate heterogeneous data and varied reporting of exercise and individual characteristics.
